gaps.sentence: I haven't got ___ cash on me — I'll pay by card.
gaps.explanation: 'Any' is the normal quantifier in negative sentences; 'haven't got no cash' would be a double negative.

gaps.sentence: ___ of the students has been given a personal timetable.
gaps.hint: this is the only option that can be followed by 'of' and take a singular verb
gaps.explanation: 'Each of the students has ...' is correct; 'every' cannot take 'of' here and 'all/both' need a plural verb.

gaps.sentence: There weren't ___ chairs, so some guests had to stand.
gaps.explanation: 'Chairs' is countable and plural, so 'many' fits; 'much' and 'little' are for uncountables.

gaps.sentence: Hardly ___ came to the afternoon lecture.
gaps.explanation: 'Hardly anyone' is already negative — do not add 'no one'.

gaps.sentence: ___ candidate was given five minutes to speak.
gaps.hint: one at a time, singular verb
gaps.explanation: 'Each candidate was given' — singular agreement; 'all candidate' is wrong.

gaps.sentence: ___ of her two brothers lives abroad.
gaps.explanation: 'Each of her two brothers lives ...' is correct; 'every' cannot take 'of' and 'both/all' need a plural verb.

gaps.sentence: She spent a great ___ of time preparing the report.
gaps.hint: fixed phrase: a great ___ of + uncountable
gaps.explanation: 'A great deal of time' is used with uncountable nouns; 'a great number of' needs a countable plural.

gaps.sentence: There is so ___ crime in this area that people are afraid.
gaps.explanation: 'So much' is used with uncountable nouns like crime; 'plenty' would need 'of'.
